facts.statehood_note: The only state formed by separating from a Confederate state (Virginia) during the Civil War.
facts.motto: Montani semper liberi (Latin for "Mountaineers Are Always Free")
facts.name_origin: The state was made from the western counties of Virginia (once called Trans-Allegheny Virginia), which split away during the Civil War. "Kanawha" was proposed as a name for the new state in 1861.

government.chambers: Senate (34 senators, 4-year terms) and House of Delegates (100 delegates, 2-year terms)
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; may serve no more than two terms in a row)
government.courts: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia (5 justices elected statewide in nonpartisan elections to 12-year terms). An Intermediate Court of Appeals began work on July 1, 2022.
government.constitution: The current constitution was adopted on August 22, 1872. It replaced the first constitution of 1863, which had been revised to include the gradual end of slavery so Congress would admit the state.
government.kid_line: "All power is vested in, and consequently derived from, the people." (West Virginia Constitution, Article III, Section 2)

long_ago.about: Ancient mound builders of the Ohio River Valley. About 250–150 BC they moved more than 60,000 tons of dirt to build Grave Creek Mound, one of the largest cone-shaped burial mounds in the United States.
Village people along the Ohio River. In the Kanawha Valley they grew corn and even used it to feed flocks of turkeys they raised.
Village people who lived in the northern part of the region around 1600, before the wars of the 1600s pushed many nations out.
The Shawnee hunted and lived across the Ohio River region. Their leader Hokoleskwa (Cornstalk) fought Virginia's militia at the Battle of Point Pleasant in 1774.

In the 1670s the Haudenosaunee, five allied nations from New York and Pennsylvania, drove other nations out and kept the upper Ohio Valley as a hunting ground. Displaced groups living in the region became known as Mingo.

first_peoples.today_note: West Virginia has no federally recognized tribes today. Few Native people lived permanently within the state's present borders in colonial times because the region was a shared hunting ground, and the United States pushed out the Shawnee, the last Native nation there, in the early 1800s.
sites: Grave Creek Mound, Moundsville: Adena burial mound about 62 feet high and 240 feet across
Ancient earthen mounds near South Charleston and Romney
Point Pleasant: site of the 1774 battle and of Fort Randolph, where Cornstalk was killed in 1777

history.event: Adena people build Grave Creek Mound near the Ohio River.
Native people burn forests to clear land for gardens, as shown by a study of a cave stalagmite.
The Monongahela culture lives in the north, the Fort Ancient culture along the Ohio River, and the Siouan-speaking Tutelo and Moneton in the southeast.
During the Beaver Wars, the Haudenosaunee drive other nations out to keep the upper Ohio Valley as a hunting ground.
Thomas Batts and Robert Fallam, sent from Virginia, are the first Europeans recorded reaching Kanawha Falls.
Germans from Pennsylvania settle the area on the Potomac River that becomes Shepherdstown (chartered as Mecklenburg in 1762).
Virginia militia defeat the Shawnee led by Cornstalk at the Battle of Point Pleasant; in the treaty that follows, the Shawnee accept the Ohio River as a boundary.
Cornstalk, on a peace visit to Fort Randolph, is imprisoned and murdered by American soldiers.
Slavery spreads west to the Ohio River. Many western Virginians resent the eastern planter elite, who count enslaved people to gain more seats in government.
On October 16, abolitionist John Brown leads a raid on Harpers Ferry, trying to start an uprising against slavery.
Virginia votes to secede. Unionists meet at the Wheeling Conventions, form the Restored Government of Virginia, and vote for a new state on October 24.

After agreeing to gradually end slavery, West Virginia becomes the 35th state on June 20. More than 32,000 soldiers serve in West Virginia's Union regiments (many from nearby states), and about 18,000 men from West Virginia counties fight for the Confederacy.
On February 3, the legislature passes a law ending slavery in West Virginia.

During Reconstruction, Freewill Baptists, working with the Freedmen's Bureau and donor John Storer, found Storer College in Harpers Ferry in 1867 to educate formerly enslaved people; it grows into a college open to both sexes and all races. Former Confederates lose and then regain the vote, and a new state constitution is adopted on August 22, 1872.

trailblazers.name: Hokoleskwa (Cornstalk)
trailblazers.text: Hokoleskwa, whose name means "a blade of corn," led Shawnee warriors at the Battle of Point Pleasant in 1774 and then agreed to a peace treaty. In 1777 he went to Fort Randolph on a diplomatic visit and was imprisoned and murdered by American soldiers. His killing angered the Shawnee, who lost an important voice for peace.

trailblazers.name: Martin Delany
trailblazers.text: Martin Delany was born in Charles Town, then part of Virginia, now West Virginia. He worked with Frederick Douglass on the North Star newspaper and was one of the first three Black men admitted to Harvard Medical School. In 1865 he became the first Black field officer (major) in the U.S. Army.

trailblazers.name: Anna Jarvis
trailblazers.text: Anna Jarvis was born in Taylor County and grew up in Grafton. On May 10, 1908, she held a service at Andrews Methodist Episcopal Church in Grafton honoring her mother and all mothers, the first official Mother's Day. Mother's Day became a national holiday in 1914.

trailblazers.name: Carter G. Woodson
trailblazers.text: The son of formerly enslaved parents, Carter G. Woodson worked in West Virginia coal mines before he could enter Douglass High School in Huntington at age 20. He earned a PhD from Harvard and became known as the "father of Black history." In 1926 he started Negro History Week, which grew into Black History Month.

trailblazers.name: Pearl S. Buck
trailblazers.text: Pearl S. Buck was born in Hillsboro, West Virginia. Her novel The Good Earth, about farm life in China, won the Pulitzer Prize in 1932, and in 1938 she became the first American woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.

trailblazers.name: Katherine Johnson
trailblazers.text: Born in White Sulphur Springs, Katherine Johnson was one of three Black students chosen to integrate West Virginia University's graduate school in 1939. At NASA's Langley center she calculated trajectories for Alan Shepard's 1961 flight and helped with the Apollo missions to the Moon. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015.

landforms: Allegheny Mountains with Spruce Knob, the highest point (4,863 feet)
Blue Ridge Mountains in the eastern panhandle
New River Gorge, a canyon about 1,000 feet deep
Limestone caves such as Organ Cave and Haynes Cave
geography.regions: West Virginia lies entirely in Appalachia: about 75% of the state is the rugged Allegheny and Cumberland Plateaus, with the Allegheny Mountains and Ridge-and-Valley region along the east and the Blue Ridge in the eastern panhandle.

ecosystems.name: Mixed mesophytic (mixed hardwood) forest
ecosystems.about: Most of the state was once covered by forests of oak, chestnut, maple, beech, and white pine, with willow and sycamore along streams. In New River Gorge, forest types include oak-hickory, hemlock-hardwoods, and cove hardwoods.

ecosystems.name: High-mountain spruce forest
ecosystems.about: Above about 4,000 feet, Spruce Knob is covered in a boreal forest of dense spruce, a cold "island" of plants and animals like those of northern New England and eastern Canada.

ecosystems.name: New River Gorge
ecosystems.about: The river cuts through every physiographic province of the Appalachians, so it acts as a corridor that lets southern plants and animals move into West Virginia, while the deep gorge blocks others from spreading east and west.

science.weather: Wet and cloudy: Elkins and Beckley rank among the cloudiest U.S. cities, and Snowshoe has rain or snow on nearly 200 days a year. Valleys often have thick fog, and the Allegheny Highlands can get up to 180 inches of snow a year. West Virginia is one of the least tornado-prone states east of the Rocky Mountains.
science.resources: Coal is a major resource; West Virginia is the second-largest U.S. coal producer after Wyoming and exports more electricity to other states than any other state. It also sits in the Marcellus Shale natural gas bed, and salt, limestone, and timber have long been important.
science.highlight: In the late 1700s, miners digging saltpeter in Haynes Cave found giant bones that were sent to Thomas Jefferson. In 1799 the animal was named Megalonyx jeffersonii, Jefferson's ground sloth, an Ice Age giant and the first fossil vertebrate genus named from the United States.

g3_ss.title: West Virginia's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Charleston and the student's county among the 55 counties; learn the Legislature, the governor, and the Supreme Court of Appeals; read Article III, Section 2.

g3_ss.title: West Virginia's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Visit Grave Creek Mound through photos, compare Adena and Fort Ancient life, and learn the Shawnee story of Hokoleskwa (Cornstalk).

g3_ss.title: West Virginia Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Anna Jarvis, Carter G. Woodson, Pearl S. Buck, and Katherine Johnson; students make a timeline and write what each one started or changed.

g45_ss.title: West Virginia's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Mound builders, village cultures, the Beaver Wars, Haudenosaunee hunting grounds, the Shawnee and Mingo, and why there are no federally recognized tribes in the state today.

g45_ss.title: Frontier Virginia West of the Mountains
g45_ss.plan: Early European explorers and settlers, the Battle of Point Pleasant, Cornstalk's murder, and how slavery and unequal representation divided western and eastern Virginia.

g45_ss.title: A State Born in War, 1859–1872
g45_ss.plan: John Brown at Harpers Ferry, the Wheeling Conventions, statehood with gradual emancipation, the 1865 law ending slavery, Storer College, and the 1872 constitution.

g3_sci.title: Mountain Forests
g3_sci.plan: Sugar maples, rhododendron, and black bears; compare a hardwood forest with the spruce forest on Spruce Knob.

g3_sci.title: Rivers and the New River Gorge
g3_sci.plan: How rivers carve canyons; model erosion with sand and water; animals that use the river as a highway.

g3_sci.title: Fog, Clouds, and Snow
g3_sci.plan: Why mountains make clouds and snow; keep a cloud journal and compare it with Charleston weather.

g45_sci.title: Jefferson's Ground Sloth
g45_sci.plan: Fossils, caves, and the Ice Age; how scientists like Jefferson identified Megalonyx, and how limestone caves form.

g45_sci.title: Coal and Energy
g45_sci.plan: How coal formed in ancient swamps, how it is mined and burned for electricity, and its effects on land, water, and workers' health and safety.

g45_sci.title: Ecosystem Islands
g45_sci.plan: Why high mountains hold northern plants and animals; map elevation zones from the Ohio River to Spruce Knob.
